title: Keep your chef plan useful as home life changes
intro: A household chef plan works best as a clear arrangement that can be reviewed, rather than a menu set once and forgotten. Your needs may change when you travel, welcome visitors or discover which dishes the family enjoys most. This page explains the practical conversations that keep the service aligned: updating preferences, reviewing portions, requesting schedule changes and discussing continuity. The details of your own proposal and booking terms remain the reference for charges, notice periods and availability, while your myCHEF contact helps coordinate the next step.

sections.title: Make changes before they become last-minute requests
paragraphs: If next week's routine looks different, tell us before the menu and shopping are finalised. A visiting relative, a new meal time or fewer people at home can all change the useful scope of a visit. Early notice creates room to assess the request properly.

Keep one current record of essential requirements and use the agreed communication channel for updates. Where a change affects hours, groceries or staffing, ask for the revised details to be confirmed. An ongoing plan should feel personal while remaining clear enough for everyone involved to understand what has been booked.

sections.title: Plan household cooking around travel and changing weeks
paragraphs: A recurring chef plan should reflect the weeks when you are actually at home. Tell myCHEF about upcoming travel, visitors and changes to school or work routines as early as possible. These details can affect the most useful menu, the number of portions and the cooking days you want to request.

Before a trip, you may prefer a lighter preparation schedule so food is not left unused. After you return, a well-timed visit can make the first few meals easier. Such changes depend on availability and the terms of your arrangement, so ask for confirmation rather than assuming a visit can always be moved without notice or cost.

Keep your food profile current when guests stay with you. Additional requirements, different mealtimes and a busier kitchen can change the original brief significantly. A short update before the menu is planned gives the chef a better chance to prepare appropriately and keeps the service aligned with the household you have that week.

sections.title: Turn your preferences into a useful food profile
paragraphs: The most helpful food brief is specific. Tell us whether you enjoy grilled fish, dislike mushrooms, prefer mild food or want a familiar dish prepared in a particular style. Examples make it easier to translate broad preferences such as healthy, Mediterranean or family friendly into meals you genuinely want to eat.

Separate preferences from allergies and other essential restrictions. These have different implications for ingredients, substitutions and the kitchen setup. Record who each requirement applies to, rather than assuming the whole household eats the same way. If you already follow a professionally prescribed eating plan, share the relevant instructions for the proposed menu to be assessed.

Your food profile should remain useful as life changes. Add a favourite dish after a successful meal, flag portions that were too generous and tell us when guests will join. Small, clear updates give the chef a better starting point for the next menu and reduce the need to explain your preferences again.

sections.title: Use portion feedback to improve the next visit
paragraphs: Guest count is only the beginning of portion planning. Appetite, meal timing and the number of dishes all affect how much food is useful. Tell us whether lunch is usually light, dinner is the main meal or family members have very different appetites. For a recurring arrangement, actual feedback is more useful than guessing a perfect quantity at the outset.

After a few meals, note what was finished, what remained and whether anyone wanted a larger serving. Distinguish between useful leftovers and food that simply went uneaten. That information can help the chef adjust quantities and choose dishes that fit the household more closely on the next visit.

If visitors are joining, update the headcount before shopping and preparation are finalised. Extra portions can affect ingredients, service time and the equipment required. Clear communication gives the chef room to plan properly and helps keep the experience generous without treating unnecessary food waste as a sign of good hospitality.

sections.title: Discuss continuity before your routine depends on it
paragraphs: A regular chef can become an important part of the household schedule, so it is sensible to discuss what happens during time off or unexpected unavailability. Tell myCHEF which cooking days are essential and where your routine has some flexibility. That information helps when assessing alternatives.

A replacement needs more than an address. An up-to-date food profile, clear kitchen instructions and a realistic first menu make a handover easier. Keep essential requirements distinct from preferences and flag anything that has changed since the original brief. This is especially useful when several family members eat differently or prepared meals need a particular handover.

A suitable replacement still depends on availability and the requirements of the booking. Avoid building your plans around an unconditional assumption of immediate cover. Ask what options can be offered if the original chef cannot attend and how any proposed change will be confirmed. Clear expectations are more reassuring than a promise that ignores practical limits.

sections.title: End the visit with a clear kitchen handover
paragraphs: Before the chef leaves, make sure you understand what has been prepared and how it is intended to be used. Identify the meal for immediate service, the portions prepared for later and any dish that still needs a finishing step. Written labels or agreed notes can be useful when another family member will be serving the food.

Check the practical points that matter to your home: where containers have been placed, which serving items are in use and whether ingredients remain for the next visit. The agreed cleanup scope should also be clear, including the work surfaces and equipment used during cooking. A good handover reduces the need to search for information after the service has ended.

For a recurring plan, note anything that needs replenishing or changing before the next appointment. For a one-off dinner, confirm how any hired items or additional equipment will be collected. The final few minutes should leave you with a usable kitchen and a clear understanding of the food and arrangements.

sections.title: Make feedback specific enough to act on
paragraphs: The easiest way to improve an ongoing service is to describe the result you want. Instead of saying a meal was not right, explain whether it was too rich, too spicy, too large or served later than expected. A specific observation gives the chef a useful direction for the next menu and makes it easier to check whether the adjustment worked.

Tell us what you enjoyed as well. A dish you would happily eat again, a helpful way of organising the fridge or a cooking day that fitted your schedule can become part of the regular plan. Consistency is built from these details, not simply from repeating a menu without checking how it is being used.

For a service concern, contact myCHEF promptly with the relevant facts. The next step may be a menu change, a clearer brief, a revised schedule or discussion of a different available match. Any remedy depends on the circumstances and the booking terms; the starting point is a clear conversation.

cta.title: Let’s shape the details around you.
cta.body: Share your date or preferred cooking schedule, Dubai location and the number of people you are planning for. Tell us what you would most like help with, and we will discuss a suitable menu and service arrangement before confirming the details in writing.
